outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of your text, refined for eloquence and flow while preserving its raw imagery, fragmented structure, and emotional intensity:

---

The redbreast kills, and kills itself again, against the window. Sooner or later, the blood in its breast will shatter the glass into hundreds of pieces—pieces you can swallow whole. Keep swallowing. The redbreast loves you, and wants you to remember that love. So it makes you retch into the toilet, blind. I was blinded by love, and drowned in an empty bathtub, spitting up birdshit, covered in red feathers.

•

Sometimes the redbreast delights in anting—with lit cigarettes, safety pins, paper cuts. God, that feels good. It wraps everything in delicate pink gauze, the color of a false sunset. Look—it is a pink soul! It wants to be naked, and it wants it to hurt. Red teeth, red toes, open mouths. Who keeps pressing my head into the sidewalk, inside the bathroom? Who keeps the lights on—the lights stay on. Who dissolves upon my tongue? Who takes flight from my fingertip?

•

The redbreast dwells within—behind your left eye, behind your right—and cleans its young with its beak. Scrubs its babies clean. Shakes its tail feathers to sweep the floor behind your forehead, and scours that floor red. My brain is a blade. My initials are beats per second, worn down to zero by the rubies in the halo. I whispered your name into the crimson air, and you answered.

---

I preserved the surreal, visceral tone and the recurring bird/blood motif while smoothing transitions, adding punctuation for clarity, and elevating word choice (e.g., "delights in" instead of "likes," "dwells within" instead of "sits inside," "blade" instead of "cutter" for a touch more literary resonance). Let me know if you'd like a version that leans even further into either lyrical abstraction or narrative clarity.

outputs.L3:
# The Redbreast

The redbreast throws itself against the window again and again, a small red missile driven by some instinct it cannot name or resist. Each collision leaves a fresh smear, until finally the impact is enough—the glass gives way, shattering into pieces small enough to swallow. This is not accident but ritual: destruction refined into a compulsion, a cycle where the only resolution is another repetition. The bird does not learn from the pain. It simply performs the same violence, over and over, as though the window has always been there for exactly this purpose.

Its love, when it comes, is not gentle. It arrives as flood, as weight, as something too large to hold without breaking. The speaker is not warmed by this love but blinded by it—vision swallowed by its intensity until there is nothing left to see but red. To be loved this way is to drown, lungs filling not with water but with something thicker, something that rises up the throat and spills out in images the color of wounds. The love does not nurture. It consumes, and what's left behind is imagery soaked in blood, evidence of having been loved too much, too violently, too close to ruin.

The redbreast has learned to find pleasure in small hurts—the burn of a cigarette pressed to skin, the prick of a safety pin, the sting of paper's edge. These are not accidents either, but chosen, savored, collected. And around each of these hurts, the redbreast wraps something soft-looking, something pink and pretty, as if beauty could disguise the wound beneath it. The suffering becomes ornamental, dressed up so that no one looking from outside would guess what lies beneath the delicate exterior. Pain, made presentable. Pain, given a bow.

The speaker begins to wonder whose hand is truly guiding these motions. Who presses the head down against unforgiving concrete, again and again, until skin scrapes and something releases in the mind? Who insists on keeping every light burning, refusing the dark that might offer rest? Who allows the self to dissolve so completely into sensation—each feeling amplified beyond reason—that identity becomes secondary to the immediacy of what the body can be made to feel? These are not questions with clear answers. The compulsions arrive as though from outside, though they clearly originate from somewhere within.

For the redbreast does not merely visit—it has taken up residence inside the speaker's mind, and there it works tirelessly, obsessively, scrubbing and scouring at something that will not come clean. It cleans the way an addiction cleans: violently, without end, mistaking destruction for purification. Over time, this scouring transforms the mind itself. The brain is no longer a place of thought but a "cutter," an instrument built only to open and reopen the same wounds. What was once complex becomes reduced to ritual, to repetition, to nothing more than the endless performance of harming and healing and harming again.
outputs.L4:
**Redbreast**

The bird comes back the way a wound comes back—
small and stubborn, breast the color
of something that won't stop happening.
I have fed it from my own hand so many times
I've forgotten which fingers are mine.

*

Some nights I press the ember there,
just above the collarbone, where the feathers
would be if I were the bird and not
the thing the bird visits.
The burn blooms slow. Red announcing red.
I call this devotion because I don't
have another word that fits the mouth right.

*

You held me like the redbreast holds a wire,
like something that doesn't know
the fence is what will kill it.
I loved you the way you love a fever—
grateful for the heat, even as it empties you.

*

In the bathroom I am learning the water's language:
how it takes what you give it
and gives back only cold.
I have knelt here before. I know this porcelain
the way I know your name in my mouth—
automatic, ruinous, necessary.

I scrub the tile. The red stays.
I scrub my hands. The red stays.
Somewhere the bird is doing this too,
its small chest working like a fist
around something that won't come loose.

*

I made myself sick trying to hold you down,
trying to hold you in,
the way you hold a bird that's already leaving—
too gentle to keep it, too desperate to let go.
I have never once done this softly.

*

Some nights the drowning isn't water at all.
It's just breath forgetting its own shape,
the lungs confusing air for something
they need to fight.
I go under thinking of your hands.
I come up thinking of your hands.
There is no difference anymore
between the saving and the sinking.

*

The redbreast returns to the same wound
the way I return to you—
not because it heals,
but because the wound has learned my shape
and I no longer know another kind of welcome.

*

Tonight I go outside and the air itself
looks bruised, looks fed on,
looks like something that's been
burning slow for years.
I open my mouth and call out anyway—
not your name, not quite,
something rawer than that,
something with feathers and blood in it,

and the air—

the air calls back.
outputs.L5:
# Sometimes

Sometimes the smallest word carries the heaviest weight. Sometimes silence says more than any sentence ever could. Sometimes we search for meaning in places we never thought to look—in the quiet of a sleepless night, in the rustle of leaves outside a window, in the space between one breath and the next.

The question of God has followed humanity since the first person looked up at the stars and wondered why anything exists at all. Sometimes people find their answer in a church pew, kneeling before an altar their grandparents also knelt before. Sometimes it comes in a hospital waiting room, when all the words we know fail us and something older than language takes over—a whispered prayer, a bargain made with the universe, a plea sent into the dark.

Sometimes God feels close, present in an unexpected kindness from a stranger, in the way morning light falls across a familiar room. Sometimes God feels impossibly distant, and the sky above seems to offer nothing but silence in return for our questions.

The truth is that faith rarely arrives as certainty. Sometimes it's just a flicker—a feeling that persists even when we can't explain it, a hope that survives despite everything urging us toward doubt. Sometimes belief looks less like conviction and more like showing up anyway: returning to prayer, to community, to ritual, even when the reasons have grown thin.

And sometimes the most honest thing we can say is that we don't know—that the question of God remains open, unresolved, and that this uncertainty itself is part of being human. We carry our doubts and our hopes together, sometimes leaning toward one, sometimes the other, always searching for the words to hold what can't quite be explained.

# What the Red Bird Knows

there is a red bird living in my ribcage and it will not stop
singing its throat full of glass and honey and I let it stay because
what else do you do with something that beautiful that hurts—

the bird was born the year I learned to hate mirrors
hatched from an egg I didn't know I'd swallowed
and now it pecks pecks pecks at the soft meat behind my sternum
looking for something it lost or something I hid
maybe they're the same thing maybe I am the nest and the predator both

morning again and the bird is louder today
red like the inside of my mouth when I bite too hard
red like the water in the sink red like
don't look don't look don't
but I look

so I gave it sleep gave it Tuesdays gave it the way my hands
used to not shake gave it every mirror I owned
still it stays still it grows fat on the parts of me
I can't name in daylight

the bird has my mother's eyes did you know that
the bird knows the exact pressure point where love turns to
static where a hug becomes a countdown
it whispers in a language made entirely of
almost and not enough and again

some nights I try to reach in and pull it out by the throat
wrap my fingers around that small hot pulse and squeeze until
silence but my hands are inside my own body now
and I can't tell which wet thing is bird and which is me
which feathers are mine which blood

there's a version of this where the bird flies away
where the ribcage heals into something that holds instead of cages
where red means rose petals thrown at a wedding
means the sun means anything
but a wound

it says *stay*

**I. Nesting**

you built your house beneath my sternum
said the hollow bones were perfect architecture
said a body this empty could hold anything

I let you
because love is just a bird
that mistakes your ribcage for open sky

there is a nest of wire in my throat now
feathers coming up like teeth
each morning I cough up down and blood
and call it singing

my hands have started curling into talons
when you're not looking
my hands have started
forgetting how to be hands

you said stay still
you said let me build
you said this is what nesting looks like

nobody said the eggs would hatch inside me
nobody said I'd feel them crack
against the cage of my own hips

**II. Migration**

something is wrong with the compass in my chest
it points only toward you
even when you have already flown

I watch my own wings molt in the mirror
watch the pinfeathers push up through old scars
like something remembering how to fly
or something forgetting how to stop

they say birds break their wings sometimes
just to feel the ground again
just to feel something
that isn't sky

I understand this now
in the marrow
in the hollow parts of me

I keep flying south into your mouth
keep migrating toward a shape
that keeps unmaking me
into weather

**III. Molting**

what's left when the feathers go
just skin
just the pink shame of something unfinished
just the memory of flight
still twitching in the muscle

you loved me the way you love a bird you've caught
gently
until the gentleness becomes its own kind of grip

I am learning to name my hunger
without shame
I am learning the word *beak*
means something that tears
means something that also feeds

there is a version of this poem
where I fly away whole
but this isn't that poem

this is the one where I lay
bone by bone by broken bone
in your open palm

and call it
nesting

and call it
enough
